doc.title: Statements
doc.paragraph: Adaptive Script allows you to execute one or more statements, sequentially. Statements are separated by the ; character. This programmatic flow lets the programmer write logic procedurally. The following is a list of the statements that are available in Adaptive Script.

section.title: Block
section.paragraph: A Block is a sequence of statements that are executed sequentially. When creating a script, a new block is created initially. Blocks can be nested inside existing blocks, using braces { }.

The result of a script is set by return, by assignment, and by calling a function that is not void. Other statements, including let, const, print(), and a script function declared : void, do not change it. If the script is only a call or an expression, that value is the result. An empty script is undefined.

section.title: Example
Assignment
section.paragraph: The Assignment statement assigns the value of an Expression to a variable, a property, or an index. You can chain assignments in one statement, from right to left. For example, x = y = 1 sets both names to 1. Compound forms such as += can be used in the chain. Assignment is a statement, not an expression, so (x = 1) > x and x = (y = 1) are not allowed. The right-hand side of let and const is still an Expression, so let x = y = 1 is also not allowed.

The logical assignments &&=, ||=, and ??= assign only when they need to. x ??= 5 sets x to 5 only if it is null or undefined, which makes it a handy way to fill in a default. x ||= v assigns when x is false, and x &&= v when it is true; like || and &&, they take a boolean. Since nothing is assigned when the test says no, a logical assignment to a const is only an error when it would actually assign.
The target must evaluate to one of the following:
This flexibility allows us to support a popular technique of assignment known as "destructuring". In destructuring, we assign an object or list into multiple variable names in one assignment.

section.title: Example
Break
section.paragraph: The break statement breaks out of the current loop or switch. You may specify a loop label to break out of that loop instead of the innermost one.

section.title: Example
Call
section.paragraph: A Call statement is an evaluation that compiles to the call of an Adaptive Value.

section.title: Const
section.paragraph: The const statement declares constant variables. Each name must have an initializer. You can declare more than one name in the same statement, separated by commas. A const cannot be assigned again.

section.title: Example
Continue
section.paragraph: The continue statement continues with the next iteration of the current loop. You may specify a loop label. The continue statement cannot be used outside of a loop.

section.title: Example
Do While
section.paragraph: The do-while statement executes a block of statements until a condition is met. Unlike the while statement, the do-while statement executes at least once. You may also put a label in front of the statement, the same way you can with for.

section.title: Example
For
section.paragraph: The for statement executes a block of statements until a condition is met. Unlike the while statement, the for statement executes an initializer, a condition, and an incrementor. The initializer can be empty, a single let, a single const, or assignment. You can declare more than one name in that let or const by separating them with commas, just as you can in a regular let or const. You can also list more than one assignment, separated by commas. You cannot use more than one let or const keyword in the initializer. Names declared in the initializer are local to the loop. You may put a label in front of the statement, for example outer: for (…), and use that label with break or continue. Labels are not allowed on blocks or if statements.

section.title: Example
For Of
section.paragraph: for (const v of values) runs the block once for each entry of an array, in order. A string works the same way, one code point at a time. Each trip around the loop gets its own binding, so a function made inside the loop keeps the value it saw. The name may also be a destructuring pattern, which is handy with entries. To walk an object, walk its keys, values, or entries.

section.title: Function
section.paragraph: This declares a function. Parameters may be simple names or the same list and object Patterns used in let / const destructuring (holes, defaults, rest, rename, nesting, string keys, and [expression] computed keys). Parameter defaults may be any Expression. Types may be written on simple parameters, on Pattern leaves, and on a whole Pattern formal. A data type on a parameter is checked on every call (see Types). When a Pattern parameter is optional, supply a whole-argument default such as = {} so the Pattern has an object to bind.

The same Patterns are already available in assignment, for-of heads, and C-style for initializers. Calls may use argument spread f(...array) to expand an array into separate arguments; spreading a string expands its code points.

Declare a return type with a colon after the parameter list (function f(): integer { … }). : void means the function is a procedure: the call is the same void singleton as print(), not undefined and not a value assigned in the body. A call to a : void function does not change the script result. An untyped function that never completes still yields undefined.

section.title: Example
If
section.paragraph: The if statement executes a block of statements if a condition evaluates to true, and the else block, if there is one, when it evaluates to false. The condition must be a boolean: if (count) with an integer count is an error, so write if (count > 0). The same goes for the conditions of while, do while, and for.
The body of an if or a loop may be a single statement without braces, but not a let or const: a declaration there could never be used, so it is an error to write one.

section.title: Example
Interface
section.paragraph: Declares a named object shape for script type checking. Optional properties use ?; use extends for one or more bases. See for syntax, examples, and checking flags.

section.title: Example
Let
section.paragraph: The let statement declares local variables in the current block. An initializer is optional. You can declare more than one name in the same statement, separated by commas. A name without an initializer is undefined until it is assigned.

section.title: Example
Pragma
section.paragraph: A pragma tells the compiler how to treat the rest of the script. #compile takes one or more options, separated by spaces, and applies them from that point on in the same script. The options turn type checking on or off and make doubles strict; Types lists them all.

section.title: Example
section.code: #compile typeCheck noImplicitAny; #compile strictDouble;

section.title: Return
section.paragraph: The return statement returns a value from a block of execution.

section.title: Example
Switch
section.paragraph: The switch statement branches control flow based on the value of an expression and the value of each case.

section.title: Example

section.paragraph: The switch statement has an optional syntax that allows you to specify a matching function through the using option. The function provided must take two values and return a boolean result. You may use any built-in Adaptive Function, or provide a custom function, written in Adaptive Script.
section.title: Example
Throw
section.paragraph: The throw statement stops the script with an error, unless a try catches it. It takes a message string, then, optionally, data and any value you would like the catch to have, and id and the name of an error. The id tells whoever catches the error what kind it is, and, when the error is not caught in a request, which HTTP status the response gets. Without an id, the error's id is throw.

The ids a script may throw are those a request can answer with: bad_request, authentication_required, denied, read_only, not_found, method_not_allowed, conflict, gone, payload_too_large, query_too_complex, unprocessable_content, too_many_requests, and moved_permanently. Any other id is a syntax error. Inside a catch, throw; on its own throws the caught error again.

section.title: Example
Try
section.paragraph: The try statement runs a block and lets you handle an error that happens in it. The catch block gets an error object with the message, the data, the id, and a numeric errorCode. The name for it may be left out, or be a destructuring pattern such as { message, data }. The finally block runs at the end in every case, whether the block finished, returned, or threw. You may write catch, finally, or both.

Errors from built-in functions are caught the same way, so a script can check the id to decide what to do, such as not_found from get_object, or conversion_error from to_integer. Throw again with throw; for anything you did not expect.

section.title: Example
Type
section.paragraph: Declares a local type alias: type Name = Type;. See for the type expression grammar, railroad diagrams, and checking flags.

section.title: Example
section.code: type Id = integer; const x: Id = 3;

section.title: While
section.paragraph: The while statement executes a block of statements until a condition is met. Unlike the do-while statement, the while statement executes the condition first and may not execute the block at all. You may also put a label in front of the statement, the same way you can with for.
